paper_a.title: Adaptive Subgradient Methods for Online Learning and Stochastic Optimization

paper_b.title: Adaptive Bound Optimization for Online Convex Optimization

metadata.description: Parallel rediscovery of adaptive per-coordinate online learning. Duchi-Hazan-Singer's AdaGrad and McMahan-Streeter's FTPRL were developed concurrently (both 2010-2011) in different communities. Both derive nearly identical regret bounds of the form sum_i D_i sqrt(sum_t g_{t,i}^2) for diagonal adaptive regularization, and both formulate the same regularizer-selection optimization problem (trace-constrained quadratic). The papers differ in framing (mirror-descent / RDA vs FTRL with proximal regularization) and in the full-matrix treatment (AdaGrad does explicit G_T^{1/2}; FTPRL handles ellipsoids by black-box reduction).

matches.explanation: Both define the standard online-convex-optimization regret. Paper A separates plain regret (DP390.3) from composite regret (DP390.5) for f_t + phi(x); paper B's DP391.1 is the standard plain-regret definition. Same mathematical object.

Both define the adaptive proximal regularizer. AdaGrad's psi_t(x) = (1/2)<x, H_t x> with H_t = delta I + diag(G_t)^{1/2} or G_t^{1/2}, centered at origin. FTPRL's r_t(x) = (1/2) ||Q_t^{1/2}(x - x_t)||^2 is a per-step incremental proximal term centered at the current iterate; cumulative Q_{1:t} plays the role of H_t. Same conceptual role (data-dependent quadratic regularizer driving adaptive learning rates) but different decomposition: AdaGrad uses a single global psi_t while McMahan-Streeter use a sum of incremental r_tau.

Both define the Mahalanobis-norm projection onto the feasible set. AdaGrad's Pi^A_X(y) = argmin <x-y, A(x-y)> matches FTPRL's Proj_{F,A}(u) = argmin ||A(x-u)||. The two papers use this projection in nearly identical ways inside their updates.

Both define the cumulative subgradient bookkeeping that drives the adaptive bound. Paper A's G_t = sum g_tau g_tau^T is the workhorse outer-product matrix. Paper B's regret-bound function B_R = (1/2) sum max_y y^T Q_t y + sum g_t^T Q_{1:t}^{-1} g_t exposes the same cumulative-gradient quantity inside the second sum. Different abstraction levels (raw matrix vs analytical bound expression) but same underlying object.

Both formulate the central post-hoc optimization problem of choosing the best diagonal regularizer. Paper A: minimize sum g_{t,i}^2 / s_i subject to <1,s> <= c. Paper B: inf_{Q_T} B_R over Q_fs = diagQ. Same trace-constrained quadratic; both reduce by Lagrangian to the diagonal-AdaGrad / FTPRL-Diag rule.

Paper A's full-matrix problem (min sum <g_t, S^{-1} g_t> s.t. tr(S) <= c) is the full-PSD specialization of paper B's bound-optimization problem when Q_fs = fullQ = S^n_+. Paper B treats it via the black-box reduction to an L_2 ball (TP391.5), while paper A solves it directly via Lemma 15 (LP390.7).

AdaGrad-Diagonal vs FTPRL-Diag. Both are per-coordinate adaptive online algorithms whose effective step size on coordinate i at time t is proportional to D_i / sqrt(sum_{tau<=t} g_{tau,i}^2). The cumulative diagonal H_t in AdaGrad and Q_{1:t} in FTPRL play exactly the same role; the projection step is identical (Mahalanobis projection). This is the canonical parallel-rediscovery match.

AdaGrad-Full uses S_t = G_t^{1/2} as its full-matrix regularizer, applied directly via mirror descent / RDA. FTPRL-Scale handles transformed-norm feasible sets {x : ||Ax|| <= 1} by changing variables xhat = Ax and running the coordinate-constant scheme on the unit ball. Both achieve full-matrix-style adaptation but via different mechanisms: AdaGrad does the heavy linear algebra (sqrt of running outer-product matrix); FTPRL avoids it by reduction to the L_2 ball case.

Identical regret bounds for diagonal adaptive online optimization. Paper A's Theorem 5 (composite mirror-descent variant): R(T) <= (1/(2 eta)) max_t ||x* - x_t||_inf^2 sum_i ||g_{1:T,i}||_2 + eta sum_i ||g_{1:T,i}||_2. Paper B's Cor. 8 (CP391.2): Regret <= 2 sum_i D_i sqrt(sum_t g_{t,i}^2). Both are the now-standard sum_i D_i sqrt(G_{T,i}) bound that defines AdaGrad-style regret. Constants differ slightly (eta tuning vs explicit D_i) but the rate and structure are identical.

Paper A's Corollaries 1 and 6 are the simplified diagonal-AdaGrad regret in introductory and main-text form, both giving R(T) <= sqrt(2) D_inf sum_i ||g_{1:T,i}||_2. Paper B's CP391.2 gives the matching bound 2 sum_i D_i sqrt(sum_t g_{t,i}^2). Same closed-form bound.

Paper A's full-matrix Theorem 7 gives R(T) <= O(||x*||_2^2 tr(G_T^{1/2}) + tr(G_T^{1/2})). Paper B's coordinate-constant Cor. CP391.1 gives R(T) <= 2 D sqrt(G_T) where G_T = sum_t ||g_t||_2^2. These are the natural full-matrix-vs-isotropic counterparts; tr(G_T^{1/2}) bound dominates 2 D sqrt(G_T) (and is tighter when gradients have low-rank structure). Paper B reaches matching full-matrix guarantees only after the black-box reduction (TP391.5/TP391.6); without it, CP391.1 is the closest analog to TP390.2.

Both establish that adaptive full-matrix-style regularization is competitive with the post-hoc optimum on hyperellipsoid-like feasible sets. AdaGrad-Full directly bounds regret by O(tr(G_T^{1/2})). FTPRL-Scale achieves the post-hoc optimum up to factor sqrt(2) via change of variables. Different proof strategies (direct trace bound vs reduction) but the end-result regret on L_2 / ellipsoidal sets is the same up to constants.

Both invoke the Auer-Cesa-Bianchi-Gentile sum-of-norms doubling inequality: sum_i x_i / sqrt(sum_{j<=i} x_j) <= 2 sqrt(sum_i x_i). Paper A uses it coordinatewise in Lemma 4 (LP390.1) and credits 'Auer & Gentile 2000; also McMahan & Streeter 2010' explicitly. Paper B uses it as Lemma LP391.5, citing 'Auer et al. 2002'. Identical lemma; this is the technical pivot that makes both papers' regret bounds work.

Both prove the doubling inequality (LP390.1 = LP391.5) by induction on T using concavity of sqrt. The proofs are essentially identical: write sum_{<=T} = sum_{<T} + a_T^2/sqrt(b_T), use IH and sqrt(b - x) <= sqrt(b) - x/(2 sqrt(b)).

Paper A decomposes the doubling-inequality proof into base case, inductive step via concavity, and sum-over-coordinates. Paper B keeps the proof as a single block (PP391.14). The first two A-steps map to B's induction; A's third step (sum over coordinates) has no B counterpart because B's inequality is already in scalar form.

Paper A's Lemma 15 explicitly solves min_S tr(S^{-1} A) s.t. tr(S) <= c, getting optimum tr(A^{1/2})^2 / c. Paper B's PP391.10 proof of Theorem TP391.6 carries out the same trace-constrained scalar minimization (PSP391.16: B(alpha) = 2 alpha + G_T/alpha; PSP391.17: optimum at alpha = sqrt(G_T/2) gives 2 sqrt(2 G_T)). Same Lagrangian solution applied to the same problem.

Paper A's diagonal AdaGrad update x_{t+1} = Pi^{diag(G_t)^{1/2}}(x_t - eta diag(G_t)^{-1/2} g_t) is mathematically equivalent to paper B's FTPRL update EP391.1 / closed-form unconstrained optimum EP391.2 followed by the lazy projection. Both compute an unconstrained step in the Mahalanobis geometry then project back. Paper A's update is a single-step gradient descent form; paper B's is a follow-the-leader form, but they give the same iterate sequence under the appropriate Q_t -> H_t matching.

Paper A's primal-dual subgradient (RDA, EP390.2) and composite mirror descent (EP390.3) are the two update families inside which AdaGrad operates. Paper B's FTPRL update (ProbP391.2) is a third closely related family (follow-the-proximally-regularized leader). All three reduce to the same iterate up to first order when phi=0 and the regularizers are matched; they differ in how the regularizer accumulates and where it is centered.

Both papers establish a generic regret-decomposition lemma that bounds online regret by a regularizer term plus a per-step subgradient term. Paper A's Propositions 2 and 3 are the primal-dual and mirror-descent variants. Paper B's Lemma 1 (LP391.1) is the FTRL decomposition Regret <= r_{1:T}(x*) + sum (f_t(x_t) - f_t(x_{t+1})), and Lemma 7 (LP391.7) is the BTRL bound. Same role: separate the 'regularizer cost' from the 'movement cost' so that adaptive Q_t can be optimized over the second.

Paper A's Lemma 16 is the per-step composite-mirror-descent inequality. Paper B's Lemma LP391.1 is the FTRL regret decomposition. Both express one round of regret in terms of Bregman / regularizer differences plus a dual-norm subgradient term.

Paper A's full-matrix Lemma 10 generalizes the doubling inequality to matrix form: sum_t <g_t, S_t^{dagger} g_t> <= 2 tr(G_T^{1/2}). Paper B uses only the scalar form (LP391.5); its full-matrix bounds are obtained via the black-box reduction (TP391.5) rather than a matrix doubling lemma. Conceptually paired, but paper B has no matrix-form analog.

Strong convexity w.r.t. a semi-norm (paper A's DP390.6) is the foundational property that makes AdaGrad's mirror-descent / RDA framework go through. Paper B avoids the strong-convexity formalism entirely by working directly with quadratic regularizers Q_t and FTRL. The structural assumption is implicit in B (Q_t in S^n_+) but not isolated as a definition.

Paper A's Lemma 8 (concavity of trace-root with rank-one perturbation) is paper-specific machinery for the full-matrix proof. Paper B has no analog because it handles the full-matrix case via reduction (TP391.5) and never needs to bound tr((B - nu g g^T)^{1/2}) directly.
Lemma 9's dual-norm comparison <g, (delta I + A^{1/2})^{-1} g> <= <g, ((A + g g^T)^dagger)^{1/2} g> is technical machinery for the full-matrix AdaGrad regret proof; no FTPRL analog.

Paper A's scaled L_1 projection (AP390.3) and bisection solver for L_2-regularized proximal step (AP390.4) are AdaGrad-specific computational subroutines for closed-form / efficient updates with mixed-norm regularizers. Paper B does not address these efficiency questions.
Closed-form l_1-regularized AdaGrad-RDA and AdaGrad-FOBOS updates are paper-A-specific contributions for sparse learning. Paper B does not derive closed-form updates for non-quadratic regularizers.
Block-diagonal AdaGrad regret (Cor. 12) interpolates between diagonal and full-matrix variants. Paper B does not analyze block-diagonal regularization.

Paper A's open problems (efficient full-matrix AdaGrad, non-Euclidean proximal extensions, strongly convex regime) are forward-looking statements specific to the AdaGrad framework. Paper B has no parallel section.

Paper B's notion of a kappa-competitive adaptive scheme (regret bound vs the post-hoc optimum) is a defining contribution of FTPRL: it reframes adaptive online learning as a competitive-ratio problem against an oracle regularizer. Paper A discusses competitiveness only informally in its remark on McMahan-Streeter (RP390.2); it has no analogous formal definition.
The symmetric-difference set F_sym appears only in paper B's bound function B_R; paper A bounds via ||x*||_inf or D_inf without naming the symmetric-difference object.

Paper B explicitly partitions matrix classes into constQ / diagQ / fullQ and analyzes competitive ratios per class. Paper A discusses diagonal vs full-matrix as algorithmic variants but does not formalize the matrix-class hierarchy.

Coordinate width D_i is implicit in paper A's D_inf and ||x*||_inf, but is not defined as a separate object. Borderline; flagging as 'none' on B side because the explicit per-coordinate width definition is paper-B-specific framing.

Paper B's separation theorem - showing a family where non-adaptive subgradient descent suffers Omega(T^{2/3}) while diagonal FTPRL gets O(sqrt T) - is a paper-specific lower-bound contribution. Paper A motivates adaptivity with sparse heavy-tailed examples (ExP390.1) but does not prove a matching algorithmic separation.

Paper B's FTPRL adaptive-norms regret theorem (TP391.2) is the master regret bound (Regret <= r_{1:T}(x*) + sum ||A_t^{-1} g_t||^2) before specializing to coordinate-constant or diagonal Q_t. Paper A's analogous master bounds are Propositions PrP390.1 and PrP390.2 already matched above; this is a re-listing for completeness, but the structural correspondence (regularizer term + dual-norm gradient term) is exact.
Theorem 5 (TP391.3): FTPRL-Diag is sqrt(2) beta-competitive on arbitrary feasible sets via outer/inner hyperrectangle bounding. Paper A does not pursue arbitrary-set competitive ratios.
Theorem 6 (TP391.4) characterizes when the optimal diagonal Q is coordinate-constant on L_p balls (p>2 vs p<=2). Paper A does not analyze L_p-ball-specific structure of the optimal regularizer.

The black-box transformation Theorem (TP391.5) is paper B's central technical innovation for hyperellipsoidal feasible sets: change variables xhat = A x, run a unit-ball algorithm. Paper A handles full-matrix adaptation by direct trace analysis (Lemmas 8-10) rather than reduction; no analogous theorem.

Operator monotonicity of square root (LP390.5, citing Davis 1963) and gradient of trace power (LP390.6) are external matrix-analysis tools used in AdaGrad's full-matrix proof. Paper B's proof avoids matrix calculus by using the black-box reduction; no counterparts.
Be-the-leader's non-positive regret (Kalai-Vempala 2003, LP391.6) is a classical FTRL building block used by paper B but not invoked by paper A's mirror-descent / RDA chain.

Paper B's lazy-projection lemma (LP391.2), projection-contractivity lemma (LP391.3), and per-round dual-norm bound (LP391.4) are the FTPRL-specific machinery that turns the FTRL update into a Mahalanobis projection of an unconstrained optimum. Paper A operates directly with Bregman-divergence inequalities and does not need these projection-equivalence tools.

Zinkevich's projected-gradient regret bound (TP390.3, external) is cited by paper A as the non-adaptive baseline. Paper B cites the same baseline in its motivation but does not formalize it as a separate theorem in the JSON.

The proof of Theorem 5 (PP390.1) is paper-A specific to its mirror-descent / RDA structure. Paper B's Theorem 6 (CP391.2) - the matched bound - is proved via PP391.6, which uses a different chain (Lemma 1 + Lemma 5 specialization rather than Bregman-divergence telescoping).

The full-matrix AdaGrad regret proof (PP390.2) uses matrix concavity (Lemma 8), pseudo-inverse arguments (Lemma 9), and a matrix doubling lemma (Lemma 10). Paper B's full-matrix guarantees come via reduction to L_2 ball, so the proof techniques don't overlap.
Proofs of Lemmas 8 and 10 (PP390.4, PP390.5) are paper-A's matrix-analysis subroutines without paper-B parallels.

Coordinate-constant FTPRL bound (Regret <= 2 D sqrt(G_T)) is the FTPRL analog of standard projected-gradient regret with optimal step size; paper A's nearest analog is the cited Zinkevich bound TP390.3. Listing as analogous to flag the conceptual pairing without overlapping with the diagonal-AdaGrad match above.
